title: Linux Command Line Handbook for Developers
summary: A chapter-by-chapter guide to the Linux shell for developers: filesystem layout, files, permissions, processes, pipes, text tools, networking, packages, systemd, scripting and troubleshooting. It ends with a one-page cheat sheet.

chapters.title: Filesystem Layout: Everything Hangs off /
points: One tree rooted at /: other disks and partitions are mounted into it, and there are no drive letters
/etc holds system config, /var holds changing data (logs, spool, caches), /usr holds installed programs and libraries, /home holds user files, /tmp is cleared on reboot
/proc and /sys are virtual filesystems that expose kernel and process state as files, e.g. cat /proc/cpuinfo and /proc/<pid>/status
Everything is a file: regular files, directories, symlinks, and devices such as /dev/null (discards writes) and /dev/sda (a block device)

chapters.title: Navigation and File Operations
points: pwd, cd - (previous directory), ls -lah (long listing, hidden files, human sizes), and tree for structure
cp -a preserves permissions and timestamps and recurses; mv within one filesystem is just a rename and is instant; rm -r has no trash, so check the path first
Hard link (ln) is another name for the same inode and does not survive across filesystems; symlink (ln -s) is a path pointer that dangles if the target is removed
find . -name '*.log' -mtime +7 -exec rm {} + finds by name, age, size or type; locate is fast but depends on an updatedb index that may be stale

chapters.title: Permissions and Ownership
points: ls -l shows type, then rwx for user, group and other; read, write and execute mean different things on a file than on a directory (on a directory, x means you can enter it)
chmod 754 file is octal (r=4, w=2, x=1); chmod u+x,g-w is symbolic; chown user:group file changes the owner and group

umask 022 masks bits off new files: files get 644 and directories 755; setuid runs a program as its owner, setgid makes new files inherit the group, and the sticky bit on /tmp stops users deleting each other's files
Common mistakes: chmod -R 777 to fix an error, running everything with sudo, and mistyping chown -R on /. Prefer the least privilege that works and check with namei -l path

chapters.title: Processes and Signals
points: A process has a PID, a parent PPID, a UID and file descriptors; ps aux and ps -ef list them, top and htop show live usage, and pgrep -f name finds by pattern
fork creates a child copy and exec replaces its program; a zombie is a finished child its parent has not reaped with wait, and an orphan is re-parented to PID 1

SIGTERM (15) asks a process to exit and can be handled; SIGKILL (9) cannot be caught and skips cleanup; SIGINT (2) is Ctrl+C and SIGHUP (1) usually means reload config; kill -TERM first, kill -9 as a last resort
Job control: cmd & backgrounds, Ctrl+Z suspends, bg and fg resume, nohup or disown survives logout, and nice -n 10 or renice lowers priority

chapters.title: Pipes and Redirection
points: Every process starts with stdin (fd 0), stdout (fd 1) and stderr (fd 2); > truncates, >> appends, < reads input
2>&1 sends stderr to wherever stdout points, so order matters: cmd > out.txt 2>&1 captures both, but cmd 2>&1 > out.txt does not; &> is the bash shortcut
A pipe a | b connects stdout of a to stdin of b through a kernel buffer; both run concurrently and the pipeline's exit status is the last command's unless set -o pipefail is on

tee writes to a file and passes the data on; xargs turns lines into arguments (use -0 with find -print0 for names with spaces); here-docs (<<EOF) feed multi-line input; sudo echo x > /etc/f fails because the redirect runs as you, so use tee

chapters.title: Text Processing with grep, sed and awk
points: grep -rnE 'pattern' dir searches recursively with line numbers and extended regex; -i ignores case, -v inverts, -c counts, -l lists file names, and rg is a faster modern alternative
sed 's/old/new/g' substitutes on each line; -n with p prints only matches, -i edits in place (use -i.bak to keep a backup), and '/re/d' deletes lines
awk -F, '{print $1, $3}' splits fields on the delimiter; NR is the line number and NF the field count; awk '$3 > 100 {sum += $3} END {print sum}' filters and aggregates
Choose by job: grep to find, sed to rewrite a line, awk to work by column; combine with sort | uniq -c | sort -nr for frequency counts; mistake: sed -i on production files with no backup

chapters.title: Networking Tools
points: ip addr and ip route show interfaces and routes (they replace ifconfig and route); ss -tulpn lists listening TCP and UDP sockets with their processes (it replaces netstat)
curl -sS -I -X POST -d @body.json -H 'Content-Type: application/json' url tests HTTP; -L follows redirects and -v shows the handshake and headers; wget is better for plain downloads
DNS and reachability: dig +short example.com queries DNS, ping tests ICMP, traceroute shows hops, and nc -zv host 443 tests whether a TCP port accepts connections
ssh user@host, ssh-keygen -t ed25519 and ssh-copy-id set up key login; scp and rsync -avz copy files, and rsync only sends the differences; ssh -L 8080:localhost:80 host forwards a local port

chapters.title: Package Management
points: A package manager resolves dependencies, verifies signatures and tracks installed files; the repository holds metadata plus the package files
Debian and Ubuntu use apt update (refresh the index) then apt install pkg, with dpkg -i for a local .deb; RHEL and Fedora use dnf install, with rpm for a local .rpm; Alpine uses apk add
Query tools: dpkg -S /path tells which package owns a file, apt-cache policy pkg shows versions, and apt remove keeps config while apt purge deletes it
Mistakes: skipping apt update, mixing third-party repos so that versions conflict, piping curl into sh without reading it, and leaving upgrades unpinned in a production image

chapters.title: systemd Services
points: systemd is PID 1; it manages units (service, timer, socket, target) and starts them in parallel based on declared dependencies
systemctl start|stop|restart|reload|status unit, plus enable --now to start at boot; journalctl -u unit -f --since '1 hour ago' follows logs, and -p err filters by priority

A unit file in /etc/systemd/system/app.service has [Unit] (After=, Requires=), [Service] (ExecStart=, User=, Restart=on-failure, Environment=) and [Install] (WantedBy=multi-user.target); run systemctl daemon-reload after editing it
Timers replace cron with OnCalendar= or OnBootSec=; mistakes are forgetting daemon-reload, using a relative path in ExecStart, and leaving a Type=simple service that forks into the background

chapters.title: Shell Scripting Basics
points: Start with #!/usr/bin/env bash and chmod +x; set -euo pipefail exits on errors, unset variables and failed pipe stages
Variables have no spaces around =, and expansions need quotes: "$var" prevents word splitting and globbing; $(cmd) captures output, $1 and $@ are arguments, and $? is the last exit code
if [[ -f "$f" ]]; then ...; fi tests files and strings (-f, -d, -z, ==); for f in *.log; do ...; done and while read -r line; do ...; done loop; functions use local variables and return a status code
trap 'cleanup' EXIT runs cleanup on exit; mistakes are unquoted variables, [ ] instead of [[ ]], parsing ls output, and not checking cd's result (use cd dir || exit 1); run shellcheck to catch them

chapters.title: Troubleshooting Playbook
points: Disk full: df -h shows free space per filesystem, df -i shows inode exhaustion, du -xh --max-depth=1 / | sort -h finds the large directories, and lsof +L1 shows deleted files still held open
High load or slow: uptime gives load averages, top or htop shows CPU, free -h shows memory (check 'available', not 'free'), vmstat 1 and iostat show swap and disk wait

A service will not start or a port is busy: systemctl status and journalctl -xeu unit give the error, ss -tulpn | grep :8080 finds who holds the port, and strace -p pid shows what a process is blocked on
Method: reproduce, read the logs (/var/log, dmesg for OOM-killer and disk errors), change one thing at a time, and check permissions, disk, DNS and the environment before blaming the code

chapters.title: Linux Command Line Cheat Sheet
points: Files and permissions: ls -lah, cp -a, mv, find . -name, ln -s, chmod 640, chown u:g, umask 022
Processes and pipes: ps aux, kill -TERM pid, cmd > out 2>&1, a | b, tee, xargs -0, nohup cmd &
Text and network: grep -rnE, sed -i.bak 's/a/b/g', awk -F, '{print $1}', curl -sS -I, ss -tulpn, dig +short, rsync -avz
Ops: apt update && apt install, systemctl enable --now, journalctl -u unit -f, df -h, du -xh, set -euo pipefail
